question: In the lecture, the norm of a partition is defined as the length of the longest subinterval. Explain why this definition is used and how it affects the construction of the Riemann sum for a continuous function \(f\) on \([A,B]\) when the tags are chosen to be the right endpoints of the subintervals.
answer: The norm \(\|P\|\) of a partition \(P\) measures how fine the partition is; it is the maximum length of the subintervals \([x_{i-1},x_i]\). Using the norm ensures that as \(\|P\|\to 0\) the mesh of the partition becomes arbitrarily small, which is necessary for the Riemann sums to approximate the integral of a continuous function. When the tags are taken to be the right endpoints \(x_i\), each term of the Riemann sum is \(f(x_i)\,\Delta x_i\) where \(\Delta x_i=x_i-x_{i-1}\). Because \(f\) is continuous, the value of \(f\) on each subinterval is well approximated by its value at the right endpoint when the subinterval is small. Thus, as the norm decreases, the Riemann sums with right‑endpoint tags converge to the true area under \(f\) on \([A,B]\).

This ensures that the Riemann sum \(S(P,f)=\sum f(t_i)\,\Delta x_i\) approximates the integral more accurately. As the norm of the partitions tends to zero, we can make \(\delta\) arbitrarily small, forcing the Riemann sums to cluster arbitrarily tightly around a single value. question: In the lecture, the integral \(i=\int_a^b f(x)\,dx\) is defined as the limit of Riemann sums along a particular sequence of partitions. Explain how the triangle inequality is used to show that the Riemann sums of any other sequence of partitions also converge to \(i\). What role does the convergence of the chosen sequence play in this argument?
answer:
To prove that every sequence of partitions yields Riemann sums converging to the same number \(i\), we compare an arbitrary partition \(P_r\) with a partition \(P_r^*\) from the special sequence that defines \(i\). Using the triangle inequality we write

\[
|S(f,P_r)-i|\;\le\;|S(f,P_r)-S(f,P_r^*)|+|S(f,P_r^*)-i|.
\]

The second term \( |S(f,P_r^*)-i| \) tends to zero because \(P_r^*\) is the sequence whose Riemann sums converge to \(i\) by definition. The first term measures the difference between the sums over two partitions that are close in the sense that their mesh sizes are small; by the properties of Riemann sums (or by uniform continuity of \(f\) on \([a,b]\)), this difference can be made arbitrarily small when the mesh of both partitions is sufficiently fine. Thus, as \(r	o\infty\), both terms on the right-hand side go to zero, forcing \( |S(f,P_r)-i| 	o 0 \). The convergence of the chosen sequence is crucial because it supplies the vanishing second term, anchoring the limit \(i\) that all other partitions must approach.

question: In the lecture, the linearity of the integral is compared to the linearity of differentiation. Explain how the property that the integral of \(\alpha f + g\) equals \(\alpha\) times the integral of \(f\) plus the integral of \(g\) parallels the derivative property, and why this linearity makes integration a less destructive operator than differentiation when starting from continuous functions.
answer: Both the integral and the derivative are linear operators: \(\displaystyle \int (\alpha f + g)\,dx = \alpha \int f\,dx + \int g\,dx\) and \(\displaystyle \frac{d}{dx}(\alpha f + g) = \alpha f' + g'\). This linearity ensures that applying the operator preserves the additive and scalar‑multiplicative structure of the function space. For continuous functions, integration always produces another continuous function (an antiderivative), whereas differentiation can fail to exist at any point, as shown by the nowhere‑differentiable continuous function constructed earlier. Thus, because integration is linear and always defined on continuous functions, it is less destructive than differentiation, which can annihilate the function’s differentiability entirely.

question: In the lecture, a continuous function that is nowhere differentiable was constructed. Explain why this example shows that differentiation can fail for continuous functions, while integration always succeeds for continuous functions. What does this tell us about the relative smoothness of the two operations?
answer: The constructed function is continuous on \(\mathbb{R}\) but has no derivative at any point, demonstrating that continuity alone does not guarantee differentiability. In contrast, the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus guarantees that every continuous function on an interval has an antiderivative (its integral), so integration always produces a smooth function even when the derivative does not exist. Thus, integration is a smoother operation than differentiation because it always yields a result for continuous functions, whereas differentiation may fail.
